The word ermine is a noun with three closely connected meanings that build on each other naturally. Once you understand the first, the others will make perfect sense.

An ermine is a small, wild mammal — the same creature that is otherwise known as a stoat (or short-tailed weasel). It is a slim, quick, predatory animal, roughly similar in shape to a ferret, found across cold regions of Europe, Asia, and North America.

Here is the key thing to understand: the stoat has two different coats depending on the season. In summer, it is brown on top and yellowish-white underneath — and at this stage, nobody calls it an ermine. But when winter arrives and temperatures drop sharply, something remarkable happens: its fur moults and grows back almost entirely white. At this point — and only at this point — the animal earns the name ermine.

One detail that never changes, no matter the season, is the tip of its tail, which stays black. This black-tipped white tail is one of ermine's most recognizable and important features, as you will see in the sections below.

So to be precise: "ermine" does not refer to a separate species. It refers specifically to the stoat wearing its white winter coat.

By a natural extension, ermine also means the fur itself — the soft, white winter pelt taken from this animal.

For many centuries, ermine fur was considered one of the most luxurious and precious materials in the world. It is strikingly beautiful: pure, bright white, incredibly soft, and rare, because it only exists during winter months in cold climates. It also had a practical symbolic value — it was difficult to obtain and expensive to trade, which made it a powerful marker of wealth and status.

Because of this, ermine fur became closely associated with royalty, nobility, and high office. Kings and queens had it sewn into their robes and cloaks. High-ranking judges wore it. Catholic clergy of senior rank used it ceremonially. It was not just warmth — it was a declaration of power and position.

The fur is typically used with the black tail-tips preserved and visible, arranged in a repeating decorative pattern against the white background. This gave ermine garments their distinctive spotted appearance — white with small, evenly spaced black marks.

Heraldry is the formal system of symbols, colors, and patterns used on coats of arms — the emblems used by noble families, kingdoms, and institutions, especially in medieval Europe and continuing to this day.

In heraldry, ermine is one of the standard "furs" — a specific, recognized pattern with its own name and rules. It represents the look of an actual ermine-fur garment: a white or silver background covered with a regular, repeating pattern of small black shapes that stylize the look of those black tail-tips.

These black markings have a distinctive shape in heraldic art — they look a little like a small shield or a stylized spot with three tiny dots above it. You have almost certainly seen this pattern before, even if you didn't know its name. It appears on crowns, royal portraits, the robes worn at coronations, coats of arms, and ceremonial dress.

There are also a few official heraldic variations of ermine:

  • Ermines (sometimes called counter-ermine): the colors are reversed — black background with white spots.
  • Erminois: a gold background with black spots.
  • Pean: a black background with gold spots.

But when someone simply says "ermine" in a heraldic context, they always mean the classic version: white with black markings.

Think of the three meanings as one flowing idea:

There is a small animal that turns white in winter → its beautiful white fur (with black tail-tips) was prized and worn by the powerful → the pattern of that fur became a formal symbol of rank and authority, used in art, fashion, and heraldry for centuries.

Whether you encounter "ermine" referring to the animal, the fur, or the pattern on a coat of arms, you are always circling back to the same core image: white, with black tips — rare, beautiful, and carrying the weight of royalty.
